concept.name: Rollup
concept.definition: A rollup is a layer-2 scaling solution that executes transactions off the layer-1 chain and then posts the transaction data (and a state commitment) back to the L1, so that the L1's consensus secures and finalizes the rolled-up state.
concept.intuition: A rollup runs thousands of transactions on a fast side system, then drops one summarized receipt onto Ethereum — the L1 keeps the evidence needed to check or reconstruct everything.
concept.mechanics: An operator batches offchain transactions, executes them, and publishes compressed data (as calldata or blobs) plus a new state root to an L1 rollup contract. Optimistic rollups assume validity and allow fraud challenges; zero-knowledge rollups attach a validity proof. Because the data lives on L1, anyone can reconstruct the rollup state and force exits.
concept.failure_modes: Centralized sequencers can censor or reorder transactions; if data posting stops or the prover/fraud-proof system fails, users may be unable to exit; upgrade keys and admin controls on rollup contracts introduce trust assumptions.
concept.misconceptions: Posting data to L1 does not mean the L1 re-executes the transactions — execution happens offchain and the L1 stores evidence. Rollup transactions are not 'instantly final' — they finalize only when the L1 accepts the batch (and, for optimistic rollups, the challenge window closes).
concept.example: An Ethereum block targeting 15M gas can carry roughly 78,000 compressed rollup transactions per block in theory; a rollup batching 2,000 transfers per post gives users cent-level fees while Ethereum's validators secure the data.
